# Pattern Catalogue

Every pattern family that bears on system design — **78 patterns** across five families — listed so that what is *not* covered stays visible.

| Family | Count | Level | Depth here |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Gang of Four](#gang-of-four) | 23 | Objects and classes | Full entries |
| [Enterprise integration](#enterprise-integration-patterns) | 17 | Messages between services | Index |
| [Distributed systems](#distributed-systems-patterns) | 17 | Nodes and data | Index |
| [Resilience](#resilience-patterns) | 12 | Behaviour under failure | Index |
| [Deployment](#deployment-patterns) | 9 | Change without downtime | Index |

Each Gang of Four entry carries **what · where · how · why · advantages · disadvantages · trade-off**, plus two fields you will not find in a normal reference: the *distributed counterpart*, and *what the top 1% do differently*. The other four families are indexed here and get full entries as their pages land — see [ROADMAP](../ROADMAP.md).

## Why Gang of Four is in a system design repository

Most system design material drops these on the grounds that they are "just object-oriented design". That throws away the most useful thing about them.

**Nearly every GoF pattern has a distributed counterpart, and the counterpart is harder for the same reason every time:** the single-process version quietly relies on shared memory and a single clock. The distributed version has neither.

| In one process | Across a cluster | What distribution added |
|---|---|---|
| Singleton — a static field | Leader election | Consensus, leases, fencing tokens, and two nodes that can both believe they hold it |
| Observer — a method call that cannot fail | Pub/sub | Delivery is not guaranteed, order is not guaranteed, the subscriber may be down |
| Memento — copy some fields | Distributed snapshot | "A moment in time" stops existing without coordination |
| Iterator — walk an array | Cursor pagination | The collection changes while you walk it |
| Mediator — a coordinating object | Message broker | It is now the availability ceiling for everything it mediates |

Reading that table is the fastest way to see what distribution actually costs.

## Creational

How objects get made.

### Singleton

**Exactly one instance of a type, globally reachable.**

- **Where** — Logger and config objects in almost every codebase; connection pools.
- **How** — A private constructor and a static accessor that lazily creates and caches the instance.
- **Why** — Some resources genuinely must be unique — one connection pool, one metrics registry — and creating a second silently doubles the resource.
- **Advantages** — Guarantees uniqueness; avoids repeatedly constructing something expensive.
- **Disadvantages** — Global mutable state. Hidden dependencies that do not appear in any signature. Hostile to testing, because tests cannot substitute or reset it. Thread-safety is easy to get wrong.
- **Trade-off** — *Uniqueness bought with global state and untestability.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Leader election · distributed lock  
> One process needs a static field. A cluster needs consensus, a lease and a fencing token — and during a partition two nodes can both believe they are the singleton.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They mostly do not use it. They register a single instance in a dependency-injection container instead — you still get one instance, but it arrives as a constructor argument, so it is visible, substitutable in tests, and has an obvious lifetime. When they *do* use the classic form, it is for something with no state worth resetting. The tell that it is being misused: a test that passes alone and fails in a suite.

### Factory Method

**A method that creates objects, letting subclasses decide the concrete type.**

- **Where** — Framework extension points; `Iterator` creation in collection libraries.
- **How** — Define a creation method in a base class; subclasses override it to return their own type.
- **Why** — Callers should depend on an interface, not on a constructor for a concrete class.
- **Advantages** — Decouples construction from use; new types need no caller changes.
- **Disadvantages** — A class per variant. Indirection that is not worth it when there are only two cases.
- **Trade-off** — *Flexibility bought with indirection.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Service discovery · DI container  
> 'Which implementation' becomes 'which instance, and is it healthy right now'.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They add it when the *second* variant appears, not in anticipation of one. A factory with a single implementation is speculative generality — the cost is paid now, the benefit may never arrive. They also prefer a plain function over a class hierarchy when the language allows it.

### Abstract Factory

**Create families of related objects without naming their concrete classes.**

- **Where** — Cross-platform UI toolkits; cloud-provider abstraction layers.
- **How** — An interface with several creation methods; each concrete factory returns a matched set.
- **Why** — Some objects only work together — a Windows button with a Windows scrollbar — and mixing families breaks things.
- **Advantages** — Guarantees a consistent family; swapping the whole set is one line.
- **Disadvantages** — Adding a new *product* to the family changes every factory. Heavy for small variation.
- **Trade-off** — *Family consistency bought with rigidity.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Cloud provider abstraction · driver families  
> The families differ in what they can do, not just in what they are called.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They are sceptical of it for cloud abstraction specifically. Providers differ in *capability*, not only in naming, so the abstraction leaks the moment one lacks a primitive — and you end up with the intersection of every provider's features, which is worse than picking one. They use it where the families are genuinely symmetric, and accept lock-in where they are not.

### Builder

**Construct a complex object step by step, separating construction from representation.**

- **Where** — HTTP request builders; query builders; `StringBuilder`.
- **How** — A builder accumulates parameters through chained calls, then produces the object.
- **Why** — Constructors with many optional parameters become unreadable and error-prone — two adjacent booleans are a bug waiting to happen.
- **Advantages** — Readable at the call site; supports immutability; validates once at build time.
- **Disadvantages** — More code than a constructor. An unbuilt builder is an easy thing to leave dangling.
- **Trade-off** — *Call-site clarity bought with boilerplate.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Fluent request builders · infrastructure-as-code  
> A half-built distributed resource is already running and already costing money.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They validate in `build()`, not in each setter, so the object cannot exist in an invalid state — and they make the built object immutable. The version that quietly causes bugs is a reusable builder whose state leaks between builds.

### Prototype

**Create new objects by cloning an existing instance.**

- **Where** — Container images; VM templates; database snapshots; game entity spawning.
- **How** — The object exposes a `clone()` that copies its own state.
- **Why** — Sometimes construction is expensive but copying is cheap — or the desired initial state only exists at runtime.
- **Advantages** — Avoids expensive setup; captures runtime-configured state.
- **Disadvantages** — Deep versus shallow copy is a persistent source of bugs. Cloning objects holding handles, locks or connections is usually wrong.
- **Trade-off** — *Cheap creation bought with copy-semantics hazards.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Container images · VM templates · snapshots  
> Cloning state is easy; cloning identity is not. The clone must not inherit leases or client connections.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They ask what the clone must *not* inherit — identity, connections, locks, caches — and explicitly reset those. The classic production bug is a cloned object that inherited the original's open connection or its ID.

## Structural

How objects are composed.

### Adapter

**Convert one interface into another the caller expects.**

- **Where** — ORM drivers; payment gateway integrations; anti-corruption layers.
- **How** — Wrap the incompatible object and translate calls.
- **Why** — You do not control the third-party interface, and you do not want its shape leaking through your codebase.
- **Advantages** — Integrates incompatible code without modifying either side; contains the foreign model.
- **Disadvantages** — An extra layer to maintain. Can hide semantic mismatches that are not merely syntactic.
- **Trade-off** — *Compatibility bought with a translation layer.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Anti-corruption layer · protocol translation  
> The adapter now fails independently of both sides it adapts.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They use it as a boundary for the *domain model*, not just for method signatures — a true anti-corruption layer. The failure they avoid: an adapter that mirrors the vendor's model one-to-one, which spreads the vendor's concepts through your code while adding a layer.

### Bridge

**Separate an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently.**

- **Where** — JDBC and database drivers; rendering backends; storage interfaces.
- **How** — The abstraction holds a reference to an implementation interface; both hierarchies evolve separately.
- **Why** — Without it, `N` abstractions × `M` implementations means `N×M` classes.
- **Advantages** — Collapses a combinatorial class explosion to `N+M`; either side changes alone.
- **Disadvantages** — Indirection, and an abstraction that must genuinely fit every implementation.
- **Trade-off** — *Independent variation bought with an extra indirection.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Storage/driver interfaces · pluggable backends  
> Implementations differ in failure modes, not only in method bodies.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They reach for it only when both axes are *actually* varying. Most codebases have one implementation and will always have one, and a bridge there is pure cost.

### Composite

**Treat individual objects and compositions of them uniformly.**

- **Where** — File system trees; UI component trees; nested permission groups.
- **How** — Leaf and container implement the same interface; the container delegates to children.
- **Why** — Callers should not need to know whether they hold one thing or a thousand.
- **Advantages** — Uniform treatment; recursive structures become natural.
- **Disadvantages** — The interface becomes the union of leaf and container needs, so leaves get methods that make no sense for them. Recursion depth and cycles are real hazards.
- **Trade-off** — *Uniformity bought with a weakened interface.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Scatter-gather · fan-out aggregation  
> A composite call takes the slowest member's latency, every time — *The Tail at Scale*.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They guard the depth and detect cycles, because the production failure is a stack overflow on user-supplied nesting. Distributed, they know a scatter-gather composite is as slow as its slowest member — every single time.

### Decorator

**Attach behaviour to an object dynamically, without changing its type.**

- **Where** — HTTP middleware; Java I/O streams; service mesh sidecars.
- **How** — Wrap the object in something implementing the same interface, adding behaviour around calls.
- **Why** — Subclassing for every combination of optional behaviours explodes combinatorially.
- **Advantages** — Compose behaviour at runtime; each concern stays separate.
- **Disadvantages** — Deep wrapping is very hard to debug — a stack trace forty frames of wrappers deep tells you nothing. Order matters and is invisible at the call site.
- **Trade-off** — *Composability bought with debuggability.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Middleware · service mesh sidecar · filter chain  
> Each decorator is now a network hop with its own latency and its own failure mode.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They keep the chain shallow and make the order explicit and reviewable, because auth-then-log and log-then-auth are different systems. In middleware they know the ordering *is* the security model.

### Facade

**One simplified interface over a complex subsystem.**

- **Where** — API gateways; SDK entry points; backend-for-frontend.
- **How** — A single class exposing the few operations callers actually need.
- **Why** — Subsystems accumulate surface area that most callers should never see.
- **Advantages** — Reduces coupling; gives newcomers one obvious entry point.
- **Disadvantages** — Can become a god object. Hides capability that some caller eventually needs, producing pressure to leak the subsystem back out.
- **Trade-off** — *Simplicity bought with hidden capability.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** API gateway · backend-for-frontend  
> It becomes a single point of failure and a release bottleneck for every team behind it.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They keep the subsystem reachable for the callers who need it, rather than making the facade the only door. Distributed, they watch for the facade becoming both a single point of failure and a deployment bottleneck for every team behind it.

### Flyweight

**Share common state across many objects instead of duplicating it.**

- **Where** — String interning; glyph caches; connection pools.
- **How** — Split intrinsic (shared) from extrinsic (per-use) state; cache and reuse the intrinsic part.
- **Why** — Millions of near-identical objects exhaust memory when each carries its own copy.
- **Advantages** — Large memory savings when duplication is genuinely high.
- **Disadvantages** — Shared state must be immutable or you have introduced a data race. Complicates the object model for what is often a modest saving.
- **Trade-off** — *Memory bought with shared-mutability risk.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Connection pooling · shared caches · interning  
> Shared state across processes needs invalidation; a pooled connection can be stale in ways an interned string never is.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They measure first. It is a real win at millions of objects and pure complexity at thousands. Its distributed descendant — connection pooling — they *always* use, and they size it with Little's Law rather than by copying a default.

### Proxy

**A stand-in that controls access to another object.**

- **Where** — Reverse proxies; lazy-loading ORM entities; sidecars; read-through caches.
- **How** — Same interface as the subject; intercepts calls to add laziness, access control, caching or remoting.
- **Why** — You want to intervene between caller and subject without either knowing.
- **Advantages** — Adds cross-cutting behaviour transparently.
- **Disadvantages** — Transparency is the danger: a call that looks local is a network round trip, or triggers a lazy load. This is exactly the N+1 query problem.
- **Trade-off** — *Transparency bought with hidden cost.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Reverse proxy · sidecar · read-through cache  
> A remote proxy can be reachable while its subject is not — exactly the case needing a timeout and a circuit breaker.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They make the expensive case *visible* rather than seamless. An ORM lazy-loading proxy that silently issues a query per loop iteration is the single most common performance bug in web applications, and it exists because the proxy hid the cost perfectly.

## Behavioural

How objects collaborate.

### Chain of Responsibility

**Pass a request along a chain until a handler deals with it.**

- **Where** — HTTP middleware pipelines; Netflix Zuul filters; event bubbling in UIs.
- **How** — Each handler either processes the request or forwards it to the next.
- **Why** — The sender should not know which handler will act, or how many exist.
- **Advantages** — Handlers are added and reordered without touching the sender.
- **Disadvantages** — A request can fall off the end unhandled. Debugging means tracing the whole chain.
- **Trade-off** — *Decoupling bought with control-flow opacity.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Middleware pipeline · filter chain  
> A handler mid-chain can be slow rather than absent, and the chain has no natural timeout.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They always define terminal behaviour, so nothing silently falls through, and they make the chain order explicit configuration rather than registration-order accident. In middleware the order is the security model, so it gets reviewed like one.

### Command

**Encapsulate a request as an object.**

- **Where** — Undo/redo stacks; job queues; event sourcing; CQRS write side.
- **How** — Wrap the action and its parameters in an object with an `execute()`.
- **Why** — Requests need to be queued, logged, retried, scheduled or undone — none of which is possible with a bare method call.
- **Advantages** — Enables undo, queueing, retry, audit and replay.
- **Disadvantages** — A class per action. Serialised commands must stay compatible with future code.
- **Trade-off** — *Deferability bought with indirection and versioning obligations.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Message · job · event sourcing  
> A serialised command outlives its sender: it must be versioned, idempotent and replay-safe.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They treat a serialised command as a **permanent public API**. A command written today may be replayed in two years by code that does not exist yet, so it is versioned from day one and never has a field's meaning quietly changed. That discipline is what makes event sourcing survivable.

### Interpreter

**Represent a grammar and evaluate sentences in it.**

- **Where** — SQL engines; regular expressions; rules engines; query DSLs.
- **How** — Model grammar rules as a class hierarchy; evaluate recursively over the tree.
- **Why** — Some problems are best expressed in a small language rather than in code.
- **Advantages** — Users express intent declaratively; the language can be optimised independently.
- **Disadvantages** — Grammars grow. A hand-rolled interpreter becomes a maintenance burden fast, and performance is usually poor without a compilation step.
- **Trade-off** — *Expressiveness bought with a language to maintain forever.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Query planners · SQL and DSL execution  
> The same query has different optimal plans on different shards.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They resist writing one. A configuration DSL becomes Turing-complete by accident, and then you own a programming language you never meant to design. When it is genuinely warranted they use an existing grammar or parser generator.

### Iterator

**Traverse a collection without exposing its internal structure.**

- **Where** — Every standard library; database cursors; paginated APIs.
- **How** — An object holding traversal position, with `next()` and `hasNext()`.
- **Why** — Callers should not depend on whether it is an array, a tree or a stream.
- **Advantages** — Uniform traversal; supports laziness and infinite sequences.
- **Disadvantages** — Concurrent modification during traversal. State that must be cleaned up.
- **Trade-off** — *Abstraction bought with lifetime and concurrency concerns.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Cursor pagination · scroll APIs  
> The collection changes mid-traversal; offset pagination silently skips and duplicates.

**What the top 1% do differently.** In distributed systems they insist on **cursor** pagination over offset pagination. Offset pagination silently skips and duplicates rows when the underlying data changes mid-traversal, and the bug is invisible in testing because test data does not move. This one distinction separates people who have run a paginated API in production from people who have not.

### Mediator

**Objects communicate through a hub rather than directly with each other.**

- **Where** — Message brokers; saga orchestrators; UI dialog coordinators; air traffic control.
- **How** — A mediator holds the interaction rules; participants only know the mediator.
- **Why** — `N` objects talking directly to each other is `N²` couplings, and every one is a reason to redeploy something.
- **Advantages** — Collapses `N²` couplings to `N`; interaction logic lives in one reviewable place.
- **Disadvantages** — The mediator accumulates all the complexity it removed from everyone else, and becomes a god object. It is also, distributed, a single point of failure.
- **Trade-off** — *Decoupling bought by concentrating complexity in one place.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Message broker · orchestrator · saga coordinator  
> It becomes the availability ceiling for everything it mediates.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They watch for the mediator becoming the thing nobody dares change. Distributed, the critical question is one most people skip: **is the mediator itself redundant?** A message broker mediating twelve services caps all twelve at its own availability, and it is routinely the least redundant thing in the diagram.

### Memento

**Capture and restore an object's state without violating encapsulation.**

- **Where** — Undo stacks; database savepoints; consumer offsets; VM snapshots.
- **How** — The object produces an opaque snapshot only it can interpret.
- **Why** — Rollback requires saved state, but exposing internals to save them breaks encapsulation.
- **Advantages** — Undo without leaking internals.
- **Disadvantages** — Memory cost per snapshot. Snapshots go stale as the class evolves.
- **Trade-off** — *Reversibility bought with storage and versioning.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Snapshots · checkpoints · consumer offsets  
> A distributed snapshot is not a single moment unless coordinated (Chandy–Lamport).

**What the top 1% do differently.** They snapshot *deltas* rather than full state where they can, and version the snapshot format. Distributed, they know a snapshot across nodes is not a moment in time unless it is coordinated — which is what Chandy–Lamport exists for, and why 'just snapshot everything at midnight' is not a backup strategy.

### Observer

**Notify dependents automatically when an object changes state.**

- **Where** — Pub/sub; webhooks; UI data binding; change data capture.
- **How** — Subjects keep a subscriber list and call each on change.
- **Why** — Publishers should not need to know who cares.
- **Advantages** — Loose coupling; subscribers added without touching the publisher.
- **Disadvantages** — Notification order is unspecified. Cascading updates are hard to trace. **Subscribers that are never removed are a classic memory leak.**
- **Trade-off** — *Decoupling bought with untraceable control flow.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Pub/sub · webhooks · change data capture  
> Delivery and ordering are not guaranteed and the observer may be down. In-process this was a method call that could not fail.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They treat unsubscription as a lifecycle obligation, because the leak is silent and only appears under sustained load. Distributed, they know the in-process version cannot fail and the distributed version fails constantly — delivery is not guaranteed, ordering is not guaranteed, and the observer may be down. Every webhook needs retry, idempotency and a DLQ.

### State

**Change an object's behaviour when its internal state changes.**

- **Where** — Order lifecycles; connection state machines; workflow engines like Temporal.
- **How** — Each state is an object; the context delegates and states control transitions.
- **Why** — Large conditionals over a status field become unmaintainable and permit illegal transitions.
- **Advantages** — Illegal transitions become impossible rather than merely discouraged; each state is testable alone.
- **Disadvantages** — A class per state. Overkill for two or three states.
- **Trade-off** — *Correctness bought with class count.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Workflow engines · Step Functions · Temporal  
> Transitions must be durable and exactly-once, or a crash lands you in an undefined state.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They draw the diagram first and treat *missing* arrows as the specification — the value is in the transitions you have made unrepresentable. Distributed, transitions must be durable and exactly-once, because a crash mid-transition leaves the machine in a state that does not appear on the diagram at all.

### Strategy

**Select an interchangeable algorithm at runtime.**

- **Where** — Load balancing algorithms; compression codec selection; pricing rules; sort comparators.
- **How** — Encapsulate each algorithm behind a common interface; inject the chosen one.
- **Why** — Hard-coded conditionals over algorithm choice are rigid and untestable in isolation.
- **Advantages** — Algorithms swap without touching callers; each is testable alone.
- **Disadvantages** — Callers must know enough to choose. A class per algorithm.
- **Trade-off** — *Flexibility bought with a choice the caller now has to make.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Load balancing algorithms · routing and placement policy  
> The right strategy depends on live conditions the caller cannot observe.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They make the *default* correct and the choice rare, rather than exposing a menu. In load balancing they know least-connections usually beats round-robin for heterogeneous request costs — and that the right strategy depends on live conditions the caller cannot see, which is an argument for choosing adaptively rather than configuring.

### Template Method

**A base class defines the skeleton; subclasses fill in steps.**

- **Where** — Framework lifecycle hooks; test setup/teardown; MapReduce.
- **How** — A non-overridable method calls overridable steps in a fixed order.
- **Why** — Several variants share a sequence but differ in individual steps.
- **Advantages** — Removes duplication; the shared sequence is enforced, not merely documented.
- **Disadvantages** — Inheritance-based, so it is rigid — subclasses are bound to the base's shape. Deep hierarchies become opaque.
- **Trade-off** — *Shared structure bought with inheritance coupling.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** Framework hooks · pipeline stages · MapReduce  
> One slow or failing step stalls every stage behind it.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They prefer composition — pass the steps in as functions — because it composes and tests better than a hierarchy. Distributed, one slow step stalls every stage behind it, which is why pipelines need per-stage timeouts.

### Visitor

**Add operations to an object structure without modifying its classes.**

- **Where** — AST traversal in compilers; linters; schema migration tooling.
- **How** — Elements accept a visitor and dispatch to the method for their type.
- **Why** — You need new operations over a stable structure, and editing every class for each new operation does not scale.
- **Advantages** — New operations without touching the elements; related logic stays together.
- **Disadvantages** — **Adding a new element type breaks every visitor.** Double dispatch is awkward in most languages and unfamiliar to most readers.
- **Trade-off** — *Operation extensibility bought with element rigidity.*

> **Distributed counterpart:** AST/query traversal · schema migration tooling  
> The structure is distributed, so traversal is a distributed algorithm with partial failure.

**What the top 1% do differently.** They apply the rule that decides it: use Visitor when the *structure* is stable and the *operations* churn; if new element types appear regularly, it is the wrong pattern and will punish you on every addition. In languages with pattern matching they use that instead.

## Enterprise integration patterns

Hohpe & Woolf. The vocabulary of anything message-based — and the reason "just put a queue in front of it" is not a design.

| Pattern | Intent | Seen as |
|---|---|---|
| **Message Channel** | A named conduit between producer and consumer | queue, topic |
| **Point-to-Point Channel** | Exactly one consumer receives each message | SQS, RabbitMQ queue |
| **Publish-Subscribe** | Every subscriber receives every message | SNS, Kafka topic |
| **Message Router** | Route by content or header | Kafka partitioner, exchange bindings |
| **Content-Based Router** | Route on payload contents | event routing rules |
| **Message Translator** | Convert between formats | schema registry, adapters |
| **Message Filter** | Discard messages that do not match | subscription filters |
| **Splitter** | One message into many | batch fan-out |
| **Aggregator** | Many messages into one | windowed aggregation |
| **Resequencer** | Restore order after out-of-order delivery | sequence numbers |
| **Scatter-Gather** | Broadcast, then combine responses | federated search |
| **Dead Letter Channel** | Park messages that cannot be processed | DLQ |
| **Idempotent Receiver** | Safe to receive the same message twice | idempotency keys |
| **Competing Consumers** | Many workers on one queue | consumer groups |
| **Claim Check** | Store the payload, pass a reference | S3 pointer in the message |
| **Guaranteed Delivery** | Message survives a crash | persistent queues, WAL |
| **Transactional Outbox** | Write and publish atomically | outbox table + CDC |

## Distributed systems patterns

| Pattern | Intent | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| **Saga** | Long-lived transaction as compensable local steps | `Advanced` |
| **CQRS** | Separate read and write models | `Advanced` |
| **Event Sourcing** | State as an append-only event log | `Advanced` |
| **Transactional Outbox** | Atomically commit and publish | `Advanced` |
| **Change Data Capture** | The replication log becomes the event stream | `Advanced` |
| **Leader Election** | One node coordinates | `Expert` |
| **Consensus (Raft/Paxos)** | Agreement despite failures | `Expert` |
| **Quorum** | Majority read/write overlap | `Advanced` |
| **Consistent Hashing** | Minimal reshuffling when nodes change | `Advanced` |
| **Vector Clocks** | Track causality without a global clock | `Expert` |
| **CRDT** | Data types that merge without coordination | `Expert` |
| **Two-Phase Commit** | Atomic commit across nodes — and why it blocks | `Advanced` |
| **Gossip** | Epidemic state dissemination | `Advanced` |
| **Lease / Fencing Token** | Ownership that survives a stalled holder | `Expert` |
| **Read Repair** | Fix stale replicas on read | `Advanced` |
| **Hinted Handoff** | Hold writes for a node that is down | `Advanced` |
| **Merkle Tree** | Cheaply find which replicas diverged | `Expert` |

## Resilience patterns

| Pattern | Intent |
|---|---|
| **Retry with backoff + jitter** | Survive transient faults without synchronising clients |
| **Circuit Breaker** | Stop calling a failing dependency |
| **Bulkhead** | Isolate pools so one failure cannot exhaust everything |
| **Timeout** | Convert 'slow' into 'failed', the only mode you can handle |
| **Rate Limiting** | Cap what any one caller may consume |
| **Load Shedding** | Drop low-value work to protect high-value work |
| **Backpressure** | Tell producers to slow down instead of buffering forever |
| **Graceful Degradation** | Serve a reduced feature set rather than nothing |
| **Hedged Request** | Duplicate after p95, take the first answer — buys tail latency |
| **Health Check / Heartbeat** | Detect a dead instance before users do |
| **Cell-Based Architecture** | Partition the stack so failure has a bounded blast radius |
| **Chaos Engineering** | Inject failure deliberately — untested failover is not failover |

Three of these are routinely conflated and are **not** the same thing: **rate limiting** caps a caller, **load shedding** drops low-value work to protect high-value work, and **backpressure** tells the producer to slow down. A system can need all three, and each fails differently in the absence of the others.

## Deployment patterns

| Pattern | Intent |
|---|---|
| **Blue-Green** | Two identical environments, flip traffic between them |
| **Canary** | Route a small percentage to the new version first |
| **Rolling Update** | Replace instances gradually |
| **Feature Flag** | Decouple deploying code from releasing behaviour |
| **Strangler Fig** | Replace a legacy system incrementally |
| **Expand-Contract** | Zero-downtime schema change in three deploys |
| **Sidecar** | Cross-cutting concerns in a co-located process |
| **Ambassador** | Proxy outbound calls on behalf of the application |
| **Backend-for-Frontend** | A tailored API per client type |

These belong here because the chain in [System Design Thinking](../SYSTEM-DESIGN-THINKING.md#part-1--the-chain) has *"deploys meant downtime"* as a reason the load balancer gets added. Deployment is an architectural force, not an afterthought.
